file: papers/pdf/Merton and Barber - 2004 - The Diverse Significance of Serendipity in Science.pdf
about: A sociological review of how scientists, inventors and commentators have understood the role of accident and serendipity in discovery: its definition, the prepared mind, its bearing on merit, and the conditions (planning, research organization, theory) that make it more or less likely.

candidates.label: Finding what was not sought
candidates.definition: Serendipity is making discoveries, by accident and sagacity, of things one was not looking for, often while searching for something else.
candidates.applies_when: The account describes coming upon a valuable result, idea or opportunity while pursuing a different goal.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The result was the planned target of a deliberate search; that is ordinary planned discovery.

candidates.label: Accident plus sagacity
candidates.definition: A chance discovery requires both the chance phenomenon and an appropriate, intelligent observer who perceives its significance; the observation alone is not a discovery.
candidates.applies_when: The person stresses that the chance event mattered only because they recognised its significance.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Pure luck with no recognition or interpretation by the person.

candidates.label: Art of profiting from the unexpected
candidates.definition: Langmuir defines serendipity as the art of profiting from unexpected occurrences, an active capacity rather than a passive event.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes deliberately turning an unexpected occurrence to advantage.

candidates.label: Unanticipated anomalous datum
candidates.definition: The trigger is an unexpected observation that seems inconsistent with prevailing theory or established facts, provoking curiosity and the urge to make sense of it.
candidates.applies_when: An account reports a surprising fact that contradicted expectations and prompted puzzlement.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Unexpected but unsurprising events that fit existing expectations.

candidates.label: Hint from another person
candidates.definition: The pregnant hint may come from someone else, such as a patient reporting an unexpected side effect, rather than from one's own observation.
candidates.applies_when: The unexpected lead is reported by a customer, user or other third party and then followed up.

candidates.label: Byproduct of planned work
candidates.definition: Unexpected results arise as byproducts of planned work aimed at a different product, and may become more important than the primary aim.
candidates.applies_when: A side result of a planned project becomes valuable or replaces the original aim.

candidates.label: Pursue the unexpected, drop the plan
candidates.definition: Keeping and studying the anomalous fact and abandoning the prior hypothesis or plan, pursuing the unexpected result as a new path.
candidates.applies_when: The person abandons an original idea to follow an unexpected result.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The anomaly is noticed but dismissed to stick to the plan.

candidates.label: Active noticing vs. passive seeing
candidates.definition: Others may passively see the same occurrence; the discoverer actively notices it and takes the hint rather than discarding it.
candidates.applies_when: The account contrasts the person's attention to an event others overlooked or would have thrown away.

candidates.label: Follow-up and repetition
candidates.definition: The accident's contribution depends on subjecting it to repetition, planned experimentation and perseverance, often despite initial disbelief.
candidates.applies_when: The person repeated, tested or persistently worked through an unexpected finding before acting on it.

candidates.label: Association of unrelated facts
candidates.definition: Free association and connecting apparently unrelated facts or similarities turns a chance observation into a discovery.
candidates.applies_when: The person links the unexpected event to a seemingly unrelated area of knowledge.

candidates.label: Prepared mind / stock of knowledge
candidates.definition: Chance favours the prepared mind; the gift of serendipity depends on accumulated, even forgotten, knowledge and training that lets the unexpected trigger catalysis.
candidates.applies_when: The person attributes recognising the opportunity to prior knowledge, training or experience.

candidates.label: Shared reflection with peers
candidates.definition: Chance observations are more likely to be perceived when reflection is shared with others of similar interests.
candidates.applies_when: Others in the person's network helped notice or interpret the unexpected event.

candidates.label: Loose commitment to theory
candidates.definition: Clinging to preconceived ideas blocks recognition of the unexpected; limited commitment to existing theory enables it.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes openness to evidence that contradicted their assumptions, or rigidity that made them miss it.

candidates.label: General rather than detailed planning
candidates.definition: Detailed planning is unsuited to divergent, uncertain domains; general planning leaves freedom to profit from unexpected occurrences.
candidates.applies_when: The person kept goals broad and flexible, allowing room to follow unplanned turns.

candidates.label: Controlled sloppiness
candidates.definition: Somewhat untidy work, with awareness of loose ends, lets unexpected results arise and be traced, whereas compulsive tidiness closes off surprises.
candidates.applies_when: The person kept loose ends or unresolved questions around that later proved valuable.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Indiscriminate carelessness, which produces bad accidents as well as good.

candidates.label: Personal qualities and leisure
candidates.definition: Alertness, flexibility, self-confidence, pride of work, perseverance and time set aside for reflection make chance observations more likely to be recognised and acted upon.
candidates.applies_when: The person credits alertness, persistence or reflective downtime for catching an opportunity.

candidates.label: Early-stage field
candidates.definition: Accidental discovery is thought more frequent in the early, pioneering stages of a field, declining as systematic knowledge grows.
candidates.applies_when: The person relates chance findings to working in a new or nascent area.

candidates.label: Origin of a new path
candidates.definition: Unexpected results become the starting point of a new line of investigation, or a chain of accidents links one project to the next.
candidates.applies_when: An unexpected event started a new project or led into the next one.

candidates.label: Redirection of effort
candidates.definition: Unexpected encounters may deflect a person from intended goals toward other useful things they had not been seeking.
candidates.applies_when: The person's efforts shifted to a different target after an unplanned encounter.

candidates.label: New theory or extended theory
candidates.definition: The serendipitous datum becomes the occasion for developing a new theory or extending an existing one.
candidates.applies_when: The unexpected fact led to a new explanation or reframing of how things work.

candidates.label: Patchwork eclecticism
candidates.definition: Serendipity without systematisation can yield a mass of unrelated ad hoc ideas rather than coherent development.
candidates.applies_when: Following chance leads produced scattered, unintegrated outcomes.

candidates.label: Crediting merit over luck
candidates.definition: Narrators minimise luck and stress talent, toil and preparation, insisting chance comes only to those who deserve it.
candidates.applies_when: The person downplays luck and emphasises hard work or competence when explaining a chance discovery.

candidates.label: Modest attribution to luck
candidates.definition: Narrators attribute their own success to fortuitous incident rather than intelligence, sometimes out of modesty.
candidates.applies_when: The person self-effacingly says they were just lucky.

candidates.label: Serendipity as stigma
candidates.definition: Imputing serendipity can be used to discredit, implying mere luck, passivity, lack of plan and unreliability.
candidates.applies_when: The person or others treat chance success as undeserved or a sign of incompetence.

candidates.label: Retrospective streamlining
candidates.definition: Polished accounts of results falsify the actual process, hiding the role of chance and unplanned movement from observations.
candidates.applies_when: The person presents a tidy planned story while details reveal unplanned turns.

candidates.label: Systematic search and planning
candidates.definition: Discoveries may instead be explained by deliberate, systematic methods or a guiding theory, with chance playing a small part.
candidates.applies_when: The account shows the outcome resulted from a persistent targeted search.

candidates.label: Determinism / inevitability
candidates.definition: Discoveries are viewed as determined or inevitable, likely to be made by someone anyway, so the accident is only timing.
candidates.applies_when: The person says the outcome would have happened anyway, accident only affected when.

candidates.label: Mythologised accident stories
candidates.definition: Popular accident stories are exaggerated or fabricated because they appeal to imagination and wishes for easy success.
candidates.applies_when: An accident narrative appears embellished or second-hand relative to evidence of effort.
